title: POC scoping - NovaHealth quality eval plan
summary: POC scoping focused on quality evaluation plan for NovaHealth's clinical QA assistant. Agreed on success criteria (format compliance, hallucination rate, latency/throughput), dataset sizing for tests, a set of golden prompts and regression suite, scoring rubric and human-in-the-loop review cadence. Next steps: SOW and test artifact exchange, run initial benchmark, schedule kick-off.
next_steps: Sara to send draft SOW and POC pricing by 2026-03-24
Customer to share 250 sample prompts and schema examples by 2026-03-26
Diego to run baseline hosted benchmark and share results within 5 business days
Schedule POC kick-off (2 hours) week of 2026-03-30

Mark Chen (Head of ML): Export 250 representative prompts + expected outputs; due 2026-03-26

transcript:
Header: 2026-03-20 14:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Sara Lin (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Redwood CSM); Mark Chen (NovaHealth Head of ML), Priya Kapoor (CTO), Jon Rivera (Data Eng), Emily Truong (PM)

[00:00] Sara Lin: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to make this POC scoping pretty concrete, especially around the quality eval plan. Diego and I will run through the approach and then we can align on success criteria and timeline.
[00:18] Mark Chen: Thanks Sara. We're primarily focused on a clinical QA assistant — verifying discharge summaries and flagging inconsistencies — so quality and hallucination control are major concerns for us.
[00:31] Diego Ramos: Got it. For context, most of these POCs break down into: golden prompts, a regression test set, hallucination and format checks, and then a scoring approach which mixes automated metrics and human adjudication.
[00:45] Priya Kapoor: Quick Q: do you run the POC on Redwood Hosted or Dedicated? We have security needs and might prefer VPC but initially we can start hosted if data is synthetic.
[00:58] Sara Lin: We typically start on Hosted for speed. If this scales to PHI we switch to Private/VPC. For the POC benchmarks it's fine to use de-identified or synthetic data on Redwood Hosted.
[01:12] Jon Rivera: On workload sizing: typical throughput for our expected user base is about 1,200 requests per hour during peak, average payloads ~300 tokens, and expected burst to 5k rps? sorry 5k requests per hour?
[01:30] Emily Truong: yeah, bursts to about 5k/hour, not per second, we're not real-time at that magnitude.
[01:40] Diego Ramos: That maps to concurrency and batching choices. For quality eval though we focus on a representative set: we recommend 250-500 golden prompts and 2k-5k regression examples covering edge cases.
[01:56] Mark Chen: Could you walk through how you define a golden prompt?
[02:01] Diego Ramos: Sure. Golden prompts are canonical, high-signal examples that represent core workflows — e.g., "Given discharge note, extract med reconciliation and list potential contradictions" — with a golden expected output. We ask customers to provide 200-300 of these if possible. Also we create a small adversarial set to check hallucinations.
[02:22] Mark Chen: For scores, are you using exact match or fuzzy metrics? Clinical extraction needs entity-level recall.
[02:29] Diego Ramos: We use mixed metrics. For structured extraction we compute entity-level precision/recall/F1. For free text we use semantic similarity (embedding distance), ROUGE/ BLEU as secondary, and then a hallucination signal — heuristics that compare output against source doc and flag unsupported statements.
[02:45] Priya Kapoor: Hallucination detection heuristics — can you give an example?
[02:49] Diego Ramos: Example: if the model asserts a diagnosis that's not present in the source, we flag it. We run rule-based NER alignment and if extracted entities have low overlap we mark for human review. We also run a simple hallucination score based on knowledge mismatch and confidence proxies.
[03:06] Mark Chen: What's your target for hallucination rate in the POC?
[03:09] Sara Lin: For pilot acceptance we usually set hard cut: hallucination rate < 1.5% on clinical-critical fields, format compliance > 95%, and entity F1 above 0.88 for core extraction tasks. Those are negotiable but a starting point.
[03:26] Jon Rivera: Latency targets? We have some interactive UIs where p50 needs to be low.
[03:31] Diego Ramos: We recommend p50 < 200ms and p95 < 600ms for interactive flows. If you need lower we can use Dedicated pools and quantized variants. We'll capture throughput and cost impact in benchmarks.
[03:48] Emily Truong: How do you test format enforcement? Our consumer apps expect strict JSON with keys and types.
[03:53] Diego Ramos: We apply output schema validation — we run the model, parse to JSON, and count schema violations. We include format checks in the regression suite. If there are repeated failures we add stricter prompting + function-calling style templates.
[04:09] Priya Kapoor: Do you include adversarial prompts for edge cases like truncated notes or long contexts?
[04:14] Diego Ramos: Yes — the regression set should include length edge cases, truncation, conflicting statements, and ambiguous phrasing. We also include "golden negative" cases where the correct behavior is to say "insufficient info."
[04:28] Mark Chen: What's the human review cadence during the POC?
[04:31] Aisha Patel: We usually do a weekly sampling audit: 200 random outputs per week with focused review on flagged hallucinations. For acceptance we require human adjudication on any failure mode that would be production-blocking.
[04:45] Sara Lin: Let's talk timeline. If we get samples by 3/26 Diego can run a baseline within 5 business days and we'll present results + recommendation for model variant and config. Kickoff the POC the week of 3/30 and run 4 weeks. Does that work?
[04:59] Priya Kapoor: Yes, 4 weeks is ok. We'll need an SOW for the Dedicated option if we want reserved capacity post-POC.
[05:07] Sara Lin: We'll include pricing and Dedicated sizing options in the SOW.
[05:12] Diego Ramos: For the scoring approach: propose a weighted rubric. Example weights: format compliance 30%, entity F1 40%, hallucination rate 20% (lower is better), latency/throughput 10%. Each metric normalized to 0-100 and combined. We can tune weights with NovaHealth stakeholders.
[05:34] Mark Chen: If an output is semantically correct but slightly reworded, how is that scored?
[05:38] Diego Ramos: That's where semantic similarity and human adjudication come in. We calculate embedding similarity; if above threshold it's considered pass, else flagged for human review. For structured fields we prefer exact or normalized match.
[05:50] Emily Truong: What about regression testing cadence after initial POC?
[05:54] Aisha Patel: We recommend nightly runs of the regression suite for ongoing deployments, with alerts for metric regressions and a weekly review dashboard.
[06:04] Mark Chen: For the golden prompts, do you recommend mixing real and synthetic examples?
[06:08] Diego Ramos: Yes — real examples for fidelity, synthetic for edge coverage. We can help synthesize adversarial cases if you don't have enough.
[06:15] Priya Kapoor: On the benchmark spreadsheet — what columns should we expect?
[06:19] Diego Ramos: We deliver: prompt id, prompt text, expected output, model variant, tokens in/out, latency p50/p95, entity precision/recall/F1, format pass/fail, hallucination flag, automated score, human adjudication notes.
[06:35] Jon Rivera: Will you include cost estimates per million tokens?
[06:38] Sara Lin: Yes we'll include cost projections for hosted vs dedicated vs quantized models so you can compare unit economics.
[06:45] Mark Chen: Any sensitive audit logs captured during POC? We need auditability for reviewers.
[06:49] Aisha Patel: We provide logs with redaction options. For Hosted POCs we don't persist PHI; for Private deployments we support full audit retention per your compliance needs (SAML/SO, audit log integration).
[07:05] Priya Kapoor: Are there common pitfalls you see in POCs?
[07:08] Diego Ramos: Two big ones: not having a clear acceptance rubric and using only synthetic or only clean examples. Both lead to mismatch in production. Also under-sizing edge cases.
[07:20] Mark Chen: On the hallucination heuristics — do you surface a confidence score from the model?
[07:24] Diego Ramos: We pull model-provided logprobs when possible, but those aren't always reliable. We combine them with alignment checks against source docs.
[07:35] Emily Truong: Can Redwood run an initial pass with an open model variant and then upgrade to a quantized dedicated variant if we need lower latency?
[07:41] Sara Lin: Absolutely. That's a common flow: baseline on hosted open model, then move to dedicated/reserved capacity with optimized kernels and quantized weights.
[07:52] Mark Chen: For the regression set size — you said 2k-5k. Is 2k minimally acceptable?
[07:58] Diego Ramos: 2k is minimum to surface common regressions; 5k is recommended if you have the bandwidth. We'll prioritize edge categories so the 2k is representative.
[08:08] Priya Kapoor: How will you track format regressions over time?
[08:11] Diego Ramos: We produce a time series dashboard with percent format pass and show failing prompts. We'll add trend alerts if format pass drops > 2% week-over-week.
[08:21] Mark Chen: Walk me through a concrete hallucination example in the report.
[08:24] Diego Ramos: We'll include case-level evidence: source snippet, model output, difference points, and a flag that indicates unsupported claims. We'll annotate whether it was a false positive on detection.
[08:38] Emily Truong: For human adjudication, who at NovaHealth will do the review?
[08:41] Mark Chen: We'll assign a clinical reviewer and EMR analyst; likely two people.
[08:46] Sara Lin: Great — that fits our recommended process (two adjudicators for borderline cases).
[08:52] Diego Ramos: A few more notes about scoring: we can add a production-safety score — e.g., for any hallucination in a "clinical-critical" field we auto-fail. That becomes a gating rule.
[09:03] Priya Kapoor: That makes sense.
[09:05] Jon Rivera: Can you provide a template for the golden prompt format?
[09:09] Aisha Patel: We'll share a CSV template: id, prompt_text, expected_output, field_level_expectations, priority (core|edge|adversarial), notes.
[09:20] Mark Chen: For the initial run, what model variants will you test?
[09:23] Diego Ramos: Baseline: open LLM vX on Hosted; then Redwood-recommended quantized variant and a Dedicated higher-throughput variant. We can also test a fallback smaller model for cost-savings decisions.
[09:37] Emily Truong: Any compliance docs to share?
[09:40] Sara Lin: We'll share SOC2 docs and security brief, plus a sample SOW with privacy notes.
[09:45] Priya Kapoor: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[09:48] Sara Lin: Recap: NovaHealth shares 250 samples + schema by 3/26; Redwood sends SOW and pricing 3/24; Diego runs baseline and shares benchmark by 3/27; kickoff week of 3/30. Check?
[09:59] Mark Chen: Check.
[10:00] Priya Kapoor: Check.
[10:01] Emily Truong: Thanks everyone.
[10:03] Sara Lin: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[10:10] End of recording.

Notes on sample quality eval plan appended in chat:
- Golden prompts: 250 canonical prompts covering discharge summaries, med reconciliation, allergies, and follow-up recommendations. Each prompt has an expected-output template and field-level acceptance criteria.
- Regression suite: 2,000 cases across categories (core, edge, adversarial). Include negative examples requiring "insufficient info."
- Hallucination checks: rule-based NER alignment + source overlap heuristics + model confidence proxies; manual adjudication on flagged cases.
- Format checks: JSON schema validation, strict key presence, type checks, and enum constraints. Failures counted as format violations.
- Scoring approach: Weighted rubric (format 30, F1 40, hallucination 20, latency 10). Normalize each metric to 0-100 and compute composite score. Auto-fail gating rule for any hallucination in clinical-critical fields.
- Acceptance criteria (proposal): composite score >= 85; hallucination rate < 1.5% on critical fields; format compliance >= 95%; entity F1 >= 0.88.
- Timeline: sample artifacts by 2026-03-26, baseline benchmark by 2026-03-27, POC kickoff week of 2026-03-30, 4-week run with weekly reviews.
- Deliverables: benchmark spreadsheet, evaluation dashboard, weekly adjudication notes, SOW with pricing and Dedicated sizing options.
